sections.heading: Glamsterdam Sepolia Fork Update
sections.summary: Glamsterdam forked successfully on Sepolia with no issues; gas limit ramped to 200 million; builder participation remains low.
sections.body:
- Glamsterdam fork on Sepolia was described as "boring" — a smooth, uneventful transition.
- Gas limit ramped to 200 million post-fork; some clients needed updates but nothing significant.
- ePBS builder/searcher participation on Sepolia is surprisingly low: 5 active builders, down to 4 after one exited (Titan and Nico named; Barnabas unsure of the rest).
  - Major builder teams have not yet joined Sepolia.
  - Many blocks are still locally built; Barnabas was unsure why, suggesting too few proposer preferences going out.
- Mainnet shadow fork was spun up for benchmarking; accidentally raised gas limit very high and transitioned through the Gloas fork.
  - Fork transition on the shadow fork went very smoothly, including builders operating during the fork.
  - Shadow fork is now being used for testing with large blocks and large BALs.
  - Stefan plans to relaunch a cleaner benchmarking shadow fork early next week.

sections.heading: Hoodi Fork Scheduling
sections.summary: Hoodi fork scheduled for Monday, October 26 at 17:42:48 UTC, with client releases targeted by October 16.
sections.body:
- Two candidate slots proposed: Monday October 26 and Tuesday October 27, both the week before Devcon.
- Monday preferred to give more travel time before Devcon; the Tuesday slot was also significantly later in the day (~20:00 UTC vs ~17:42 UTC).
- Some teams (ethrex) preferred Tuesday due to flights, but Monday won out since more teams would be flying on Tuesday.
- Release timeline discussion:
  - Potuz (Prysm) raised concerns that cutting releases by the 16th (10 days before fork) is tight, and operators on Hoodi (including Rocketpool, Lido, home stakers) ideally need two weeks.
  - Prysm still needs to add a flag to disable the P2P builder stack and fall back to local building; easy to add but adds to the rush.
  - Potuz noted Sepolia had patch releases right before the fork because the initially announced release was not the correct one.
- Agreement: target client releases by Friday October 16, giving 10 days for operators to upgrade.
  - Barnabas noted ~95% of Hoodi validators are controlled, reducing non-finality risk.
  - PR for Hoodi fork config: [hoodi#31](https://github.com/eth-clients/hoodi/pull/31).
- Gas limit change confirmed to activate on the fork epoch for both Hoodi and Mainnet; no objections raised.

sections.heading: Retrospective EIP Complexity Assessments
sections.summary: LLM-based complexity scoring of historical forks shows Hegota is already the most complex fork before adding any remaining PFI EIPs.
sections.body:
- Dan (danceratopz) presented a study using Claude (Opus 5.5) to retroactively score EIP complexity across all historical forks using a questionnaire template originally created by Mario for Glamsterdam.
  - Template has 24 questions (updated to 28) scoring 0–72+ per EIP; covers new opcodes, gas changes, cross-EIP interactions, security, performance.
  - LLM evaluations use snapshots of EIP markdown from scoping-cutoff dates to avoid hindsight bias.
- Key findings:
  - Accumulated fork complexity roughly tracks time-to-mainnet across historical forks.
  - ~50% of fork effort comes from unpredictable work: cross-EIP interactions, unspecified edge cases, security/performance benchmarking, gas repricing.
  - When normalized to 100%, the breakdown of effort categories is surprisingly similar across forks.
  - With current 14 SFI + CFI EIPs, Hegota already scores as the most complex fork ever — before any remaining PFI EIPs are added.
- Slides: [danceratopz.github.io/retrospective-eip-complexity/slides/](https://danceratopz.github.io/retrospective-eip-complexity/slides/)
- Results: [danceratopz.github.io/retrospective-eip-complexity/results/predicted-vs-observed/](https://danceratopz.github.io/retrospective-eip-complexity/results/predicted-vs-observed/)
- Human evals also visible at [forkcast.org/upgrade/hegota/test-complexity/](https://forkcast.org/upgrade/hegota/test-complexity/)
- Mark (Lighthouse) noted that spec complexity and implementation complexity can diverge significantly (e.g., EIP-7549 attestation changes were spec-simple but implementation-hard).
- Dan's proposed next step: build automated spec-checking tooling for EIP authors — detecting contradictions, underspecification, and inconsistencies between dependent EIPs — rather than focusing on the numerical score.

sections.heading: Accelerating Fork Development with AI
sections.summary: Nethermind advocated for faster fork cadence using AI tooling; broad agreement on potential but debate on where bottlenecks actually lie.
sections.body:
- Łukasz (Nethermind) presented the case for accelerating hard fork cadence, noting Nethermind already has ~150 Hegota PRs (most merged, 12 open) and implementation is "somewhat solved."
  - Main bottlenecks identified: coordination, testing, tooling — not implementation.
  - Proposed better dashboards, notification systems, automated PR fixes when tests fail, and more tooling for EIP champions to take a "product owner" role.
  - Suggested starting headliner scoping for the I* fork soon after Hegota scoping finishes.
- Mark (Lighthouse) echoed the sentiment: in the past (e.g., MaxEB during Electra), only one client had bandwidth to assess complexity; now AI can provide initial vibe-coded specs and implementations for all EIPs, which is better than the prior alternative of nothing.
- Justin Florentine (Besu) cautioned against speed for speed's sake; urged focusing new capacity on specific priorities like PQ rather than arbitrary acceleration.
  - Supported exploring faster cadence but without forcing a fixed target (e.g., 4 forks/year).
- Ben Adams (Nethermind) agreed that PQ is hard to accelerate with AI because the bottleneck is decision-making, not implementation.
- Luis Pinto raised concerns about AI-written specs potentially reducing the value of client diversity in interpreting specifications.
  - Łukasz responded that clients must agree on core specs — diversity of spec interpretation causes consensus bugs, not benefits.
- Jochem (EthereumJS) emphasized that as AI handles more implementation, specs become the single source of truth and need more human eyes.
- Discussion timeboxed; deeper conversation deferred to Mumbai in-person meetings.

sections.heading: EIP-7907: Contract Size Metering
sections.summary: EIP-7907 added to PFI list for next call; it reintroduces gas metering based on contract size to address a DoS surface from Glamsterdam's size increase.
sections.body:
- Ben Adams presented [EIP-7907](https://forkcast.org/eips/7907/): Glamsterdam increased contract size limits (EIP-7954) but did not add metering based on contract size, creating an expensive DoS surface.
  - Testing showed contract loading based on disk speed will become the new gas ceiling.
  - EIP-7907 reintroduces the metering half that was left out of Glamsterdam.
- No opposition to adding it to PFI; decision on CFI/DFI deferred to next call (the final scoping call).

sections.heading: Hegota EIP Scoping Decisions
sections.summary: Eight EIPs CFI'd (PAY, ecRecover, SETCODEFROM, TCREATE, SELFDESTRUCT deactivation, BLOCKHASH from storage, eth/xx, receipt fields); three DFI'd (identity precompile, ML-DSA, warm access sets).
sections.body:
- **EIP-5920 (PAY opcode):** CFI'd with no opposition. Medium complexity; rated well by most clients.
- **EIP-8151 (ecRecover) and EIP-8298 (SETCODEFROM):** CFI'd together as a pair.
  - Carlos (ethrex) argued these must be paired: together they enable EOAs to migrate to post-quantum without relying on ECDSA.
  - Besu rated SETCODEFROM as C-tier but clarified they would not block it; described position as "C+."
  - Lightclient pressed Besu on their preferred PQ migration path for EOAs; Besu acknowledged the point but had no alternative proposal.
- **EIP-8360 (TCREATE) and EIP-4758 (Deactivate SELFDESTRUCT):** CFI'd together.
  - Discussed on the previous call; Milos (champion, absent) provided an update.
  - ethrex bumped TCREATE to B-tier; preferred implementing it after main EIPs are settled.
- **EIP-7709 (Read BLOCKHASH from storage):** CFI'd.
  - Initially slated as potential DFI, but Ben Adams moved Nethermind's vote from B to A after realizing it eliminates the need for 256 trailing block headers for BAL-based light clients.
  - Ignacio (champion) noted Reth's DFI was not a strong opinion.
- **EIP-8077 (eth/xx networking):** CFI'd after discussion.
  - Csaba (champion) argued it's needed for mempool resilience as gas limits increase.
  - Łukasz initially skeptical (sender+nonce alone is insufficient for robust filtering), but softened to B-tier if the EIP is made more robust (e.g., including fee data).
  - Besu supports it for future mempool filtering utility.
  - Ben Adams noted frames make mempool transaction costs higher, increasing relevance.
- **EIP-7666 (EVM-ify identity precompile):** DFI'd.
  - Felix (Geth) strongly opposed: identity precompile is trivial; Geth would just change gas price and not actually deploy bytecode; called it a "signaling EIP."
  - Jochem noted the EIP incorrectly claims no new functionality is introduced — it actually makes some inputs more expensive, and warm-account status is unaddressed.
  - Kevaundray argued it's low-risk precisely because it's trivial, serving as a proof of the precompile-to-EVM migration mechanism.
  - After debate, DFI'd as not worth the complexity.
- **EIP-8355 (ML-DSA precompiles):** DFI'd.
  - Kevaundray opposed CFI'ing three variants of a lattice-based signature scheme; lattice security concerns cited.
  - Danno argued for cryptographic agility and noted EVM-only ML-DSA costs ~1M gas, which exceeds ERC-4337's 500K validation limit and a second AA solution's 100K limit.
  - Danno proposed a middle ground: reserve a precompile address and write tests without shipping in Hegota.
  - Antonio Sanso argued against lattices: no scalability plan, mispriced for zkVM, bad timing given recent cryptographic developments; SPHINCS-based approach with aggregation (Daisugi testnet) is preferred.
  - Vitalik noted hash-based signatures are provably reducible to hash security; suggested NVMPY (SIMD for Ethereum) or accelerating EIP-8288 as alternatives.
  - Carlos argued SETCODEFROM + EIP-8151 gives breathing room to avoid premature precompile commitments.
- **EIP-8116 (Replace cumulative receipt fields):** CFI'd but placed at the bottom of the priority list.
  - Widely acknowledged as low-priority technical debt clearing.
  - Ben Adams noted bloom filter removal (EIP-7668, already CFI'd) is more impactful.
- **EIP-8374 (Persist warm access sets across reverts):** DFI'd.
  - Felix (Geth) explained Geth rated it A-tier because they couldn't find the original rationale for reverting warm sets and saw no downside to the change.
  - Ben Adams expressed concern about deep changes at the fork boundary, likening it to EIP-8037 PTSD.
  - Lukewarm overall support led to DFI.

sections.heading: Glamsterdam Ecosystem Readiness Checklist
sections.summary: Pooja requested dev feedback on a readiness checklist PR for enterprise stakeholders to report Sepolia testing results.
sections.body:
- Pooja Ranjan briefly presented a Glamsterdam Ecosystem Readiness Checklist designed to collect feedback from enterprise users about their Sepolia testnet testing.
- PR already submitted: [ethereum/pm#2266](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/pull/2266).
- Comment with details: [ethereum/pm#2234 comment](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2234#issuecomment-6060792254).
- Requested async review from devs; if approved, the checklist will be merged and shared with ecosystem stakeholders.
